p.src: Now the Great Sage Sun, vexed and dejected, rose into the air. He thought of returning to the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, but feared the lesser demons there would laugh at him for going back on his word and say that he was no true man of mettle; he thought of seeking refuge in the Celestial Palace, but feared he would not be allowed to remain there long; he thought of going to the islands in the sea, but was ashamed to face the immortals of the Three Isles; and he thought of going to the Dragon Palace, but his pride would not let him appeal to the Dragon King. He truly had nowhere and no one to depend upon. After much bitter reflection, he said, “Enough, enough, enough! I had better go back to my master. That is still the true path to the rightful fruit.”

p.src: He lowered his cloud and went straight to stand before Tripitaka’s horse, saying, “Master, forgive your disciple this once! From now on I shall never again dare to commit violence—I shall heed my master’s instruction. By all means, let me continue protecting you on your journey to the Western Heaven.” When the Tang Monk saw him, he made no reply. Reining in his horse, he immediately recited the Tight-Fillet Spell. Over and over he recited it more than twenty times. The spell felled the Great Sage to the ground, and the fillet sank nearly an inch into his flesh. Only then did the monk stop and say, “Why have you come back to pester me instead of going away?” Pilgrim could only cry, “Do not recite it! Do not recite it! I have places where I can live; I merely fear that without me you will never reach the Western Heaven.” Tripitaka said angrily, “You murderous macaque have killed living beings and brought me endless trouble. Now I truly want no more of you. Whether I can reach there or not is none of your concern. Go, quickly! Go! If you delay a moment longer, I shall recite the spell again. This time I shall not stop until the fillet squeezes your brains out.” The Great Sage could scarcely endure the pain. Seeing that his master would not relent, he had no choice but to mount his somersault cloud once more and rise into the air. Suddenly a thought came to him: “This monk has betrayed my devotion. I shall go to the Putuo Cliff and lodge my complaint with the Bodhisattva Guanyin.”

p.src: The noble Great Sage turned his somersault around, and in less than an hour had already reached the Southern Ocean. He brought his auspicious radiance down, went straight to Mount Luojia, and burst into the Purple Bamboo Grove. There he suddenly met the pilgrim Moksha, who saluted him and asked, “Where are you going, Great Sage?” Pilgrim replied, “I wish to see the Bodhisattva.” Moksha led him to the entrance of the Cave of Tidal Sound, where the Child Sudhana also saluted him and asked, “What brings you here, Great Sage?” Pilgrim said, “I have a matter to report to the Bodhisattva.” Hearing the word “report,” Sudhana laughed and said, “You sly-tongued monkey! This is just like the time when I captured the Tang Monk and you bullied me. My Bodhisattva is a holy and virtuous bodhisattva of great mercy and compassion, great vows and the Great Vehicle, who rescues all from suffering and distress and whose virtue is boundless and immeasurable. What fault could she have that you would accuse her?” Pilgrim’s heart was already full of resentment. At these words his anger flared, and with a fierce shout he made the Child Sudhana stagger backward. “You ungrateful little beast, how utterly stupid you are! When you were a fiend making mischief, it was I who asked the Bodhisattva to subdue you and bring you into the true faith under her protection. Now you enjoy such supreme bliss and longevity, carefree and at ease, with a life equal to Heaven’s; yet instead of thanking old Sun, you treat me with such insolence. I have come on urgent business to make an appeal to the Bodhisattva. How dare you twist my words and say that my sly tongue intends to accuse her?” Sudhana smiled apologetically and said, “You are still as quick-tempered a monkey as ever. I was only joking with you. Why did your face change so quickly?”

p.src: As they were speaking, the white parrot fluttered to and fro. Knowing that the Bodhisattva was summoning them, Moksha and Sudhana led the way to the precious lotus throne. At the sight of the Bodhisattva, Pilgrim threw himself down in obeisance. His tears gushed like a spring, and he burst into loud sobs. The Bodhisattva told Moksha and Sudhana to help him up, and said, “Wukong, tell me plainly what has grieved you so. Do not cry, do not cry. I shall relieve your suffering and avert your calamity.” Pilgrim, still shedding tears, bowed again and said, “In all the years before I became your disciple, when did I ever suffer such humiliation? Since the Bodhisattva delivered me from Heaven’s punishment, ordained me into the Buddhist faith, and charged me to protect the Tang Monk on his journey to worship the Buddha and fetch the scriptures from the Western Heaven, I have risked life and limb to rescue him from demonic perils. It has been like snatching a tender bone from a tiger’s jaws or stripping living scales from a flood dragon’s back. I hoped only to return to the true path and attain the rightful fruit, cleansing away my sins and casting out evil. How could I know that the elder would betray all loyalty and gratitude, blindly forsake this good affinity, and refuse to distinguish right from wrong?” The Bodhisattva said, “Then tell me the cause of this dispute, so that I may hear which side is right.” Pilgrim then gave a detailed account from beginning to end of how he had beaten the bandits to death. He explained that the Tang Monk had resented him for killing so many people and, without judging right from wrong, had recited the Tight-Fillet Spell and driven him away several times. With no road to Heaven and no gate into the earth, he had come especially to tell the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva said, “Tang Sanzang is journeying west by imperial command. Devoted to goodness in his monastic life, he would never lightly harm a living creature. With your immeasurable supernatural powers, why did you need to kill so many bandits? Though the bandits were wicked, they were human beings after all and ought not to have been killed. They were not the same as demonic birds, monstrous beasts, ghosts, spirits, fiends, and devils. To kill such creatures is an achievement to your credit; but to kill human beings is still an act of cruelty on your part. You needed only to drive them off and scatter them, and your master would naturally have been saved. In my impartial judgment, it was still you who did wrong.”

p.src: With tears in his eyes, Pilgrim knocked his head upon the ground and said, “Even if your disciple did wrong, my merits should have been set against my fault. He should not have driven me away like this. I implore the Bodhisattva in her great mercy and compassion to recite the Loose-Fillet Spell, remove this golden fillet, and take it back. Then let me return to the Water-Curtain Cave and seek a life for myself.” The Bodhisattva smiled and said, “The Tight-Fillet Spell was originally transmitted to me by the Tathagata. When he sent me to the Eastern Land to seek a scripture pilgrim, he bestowed upon me three treasures: the brocade cassock, the nine-ringed monk’s staff, and three fillets—the Golden, the Tight, and the Prohibitive. He secretly taught me three spells, but there was no Loose-Fillet Spell among them.” Pilgrim said, “If that is so, I shall take my leave of the Bodhisattva.” The Bodhisattva asked, “After leaving me, where will you go?” Pilgrim replied, “I shall go to the Western Heaven, appeal to the Tathagata, and ask him to recite the Loose-Fillet Spell.” The Bodhisattva said, “Stay a while. Let me examine whether fortune or misfortune awaits you.” Pilgrim said, “There is no need to look. Things are already inauspicious enough as they are.” The Bodhisattva said, “I am not examining you. I am examining what fortune or misfortune awaits the Tang Monk.”

p.src: The noble Bodhisattva sat upright upon her lotus throne, cast her mind throughout the Three Realms, and gazed afar with her wisdom eye, surveying the whole universe. In an instant she spoke: “Wukong, within moments your master will face a calamity that threatens his person. Before long he will come seeking you. Remain here. I shall speak with the Tang Monk and have him take you along once more to fetch the scriptures, so that you may attain the rightful fruit.” The Great Sage Sun had no choice but to submit. Not daring to act rashly, he stood in attendance beneath the precious lotus throne. Of him we speak no more for now.

p.src: Now when Elder Tang had driven the Pilgrim away, he told Bajie to lead the horse and Friar Sand to carry the luggage. The four of them, counting the horse, journeyed westward for nearly fifty li. Tripitaka reined in his horse and said, “Disciples, we left the village at the fifth watch, and then that Protector of the Horses caused us all that vexation. Half the day has passed, and I am both hungry and thirsty. Which of you will go beg some food for me?” Bajie said, “Master, please dismount and rest. Let me see whether there is a village nearby where I can beg for food.” Hearing this, Tripitaka tumbled down from the horse. The Idiot sprang onto a cloud and surveyed the land carefully from midair, but all he could see were mountains and ridges, without a single household in sight. Bajie brought his cloud down and told Tripitaka, “There is nowhere to beg for food. As far as I can see, there is not a single village or dwelling.” Tripitaka said, “If there is nowhere to beg for food, at least bring me some water to quench my thirst.” Bajie said, “I will fetch some water from the ravine by the southern mountain.” Friar Sand immediately took out the alms bowl and handed it to Bajie. Holding the bowl, Bajie mounted the clouds and mist and departed. The elder sat beside the road and waited a very long time, but Bajie did not return. Poor Tripitaka’s mouth was parched and his tongue bitter, and the torment was hard to bear. A poem bears witness to this. The poem says:

p.src: Standing nearby, Friar Sand saw that Tripitaka could no longer endure his hunger and thirst, while Bajie still had not returned with the water. He had no choice but to secure the luggage and tether the white horse firmly, saying, “Master, sit here at ease while I go and hurry him back with the water.” The elder was too tearful to speak and merely nodded in reply. Friar Sand hastily mounted a cloud and also flew toward the southern mountain.

p.src: Left alone, the master suffered and struggled on, his distress becoming unbearable. Just as he was in utter misery and alarm, he suddenly heard a loud sound. The elder started and raised himself to look. There was the Pilgrim Sun, kneeling beside the road and holding a porcelain cup in both hands. He said, “Master, without old Monkey here, you cannot even get a drink of water. Here is a cup of good cool water. Take a drink to quench your thirst, and then I will go beg some food.” The elder said, “I will not drink your water. If I die of thirst on this very spot, I shall accept my fate. I want no more of you. Go away.” The Pilgrim said, “Without me, you will never reach the Western Heaven.” Tripitaka said, “Whether I reach it or not is none of your concern. You wretched macaque, why must you keep pestering me?” The Pilgrim’s expression changed. Flying into a rage, he shouted abuse at the elder: “You heartless, wretched baldhead! How utterly you despise me!” He swung his iron staff, flung away the porcelain cup, and brought the weapon down hard upon the elder’s back. The elder fell unconscious to the ground, unable to speak. The attacker seized the two bundles wrapped in blue felt, mounted his somersault cloud, and vanished no one knew where.

p.src: Now Bajie, carrying the alms bowl, hurried straight to the southern slope of the mountain, where he suddenly saw a thatched dwelling in a hollow among the hills. When he had looked before, the high mountain had hidden it from view, so he had not seen it; only now that he had come close did he discover the household. The Idiot thought to himself, “With an ugly face like mine, they will certainly be frightened. All my trouble will be wasted, and I shall never manage to beg a meal. I must change into something better. I must indeed.”

p.src: What a fine Idiot! He made a magic sign, recited a spell, and shook himself seven or eight times, changing into a sallow, bloated monk wasted by a ravenous ailment. Groaning and whimpering, he shuffled up to the door and called, “Kind patrons, there is leftover rice in your kitchen, and a starving traveler on the road. This poor monk has come from the Eastern Land and is bound for the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. My master is starving and parched on the road. If you have any scorched rice or cold leftovers, I beg you to spare some to save him from hunger.” As it happened, none of the men of the household were home; they had all gone to transplant rice seedlings and sow grain. Only two women were at home. They had just cooked the midday meal and filled two basins, which they were preparing to carry out to the fields. Some rice and scorched crust still remained in the pot and had not yet been dished out. Seeing his sickly appearance and hearing him claim that he was traveling from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven, the women suspected that illness had muddled his wits and made him rave. They also feared he might collapse and die at their doorway. So, coaxing and placating him, they filled his bowl to the brim with leftover rice and scorched crust. The Idiot took it, resumed his true form, and went straight back along the old road.

p.src: As he walked, he heard someone call, “Bajie!” Bajie looked up and saw Friar Sand standing on a cliff and shouting, “Come over here! Come over here!” When Friar Sand had come down the cliff and met him, he said, “There is such clear water in this ravine, yet instead of drawing it, where did you go?” Bajie laughed and said, “When I reached this place, I saw a household in a hollow among the hills, so I went and begged this bowlful of cooked rice.” Friar Sand said, “We shall need the rice too, but Master is terribly thirsty. How are we to carry water back?” Bajie said, “Getting water is easy. Hold out the front of your robe and carry this rice in it, and I will use the bowl to draw water.”

p.src: The two returned happily to the road, only to find Tripitaka lying facedown in the dust; the white horse had thrown its reins loose and was neighing, running, and leaping beside the road; and the luggage was nowhere to be seen. Bajie was so alarmed that he stamped his feet and beat his chest, crying and shouting, “There is no need to ask! No need to ask! It must have been some confederate of the Pilgrim Sun whom we drove away. He came here, killed Master, and stole the luggage!” Friar Sand said, “First go and tether the horse!” Then he kept crying, “What are we to do? What are we to do? This is truly what they call giving up halfway and stopping in the middle of the road.” He called once, “Master!” Tears streamed from his eyes like pearls as he wept bitterly in grief. Bajie said, “Brother, stop crying for now. Now that matters have come to this, we need say no more about fetching the scriptures. You stay here and watch over Master’s remains while I ride the horse to some prefecture, district, village, town, or market and sell it for a few taels of silver. We shall buy a coffin and bury Master, and then the two of us can each go our own way and part company.”

p.src: Friar Sand truly could not bear to abandon him. He turned the Tang Monk over and pressed his own face to his master’s to feel for warmth, crying, “My ill-fated Master!” Then he noticed warm breath coming from the elder’s mouth and nose and felt warmth in his chest. He called repeatedly, “Bajie, come here! Master is still alive!” Only then did the Idiot come forward and help the elder up. After regaining consciousness and groaning for a while, the elder cursed, “That wretched macaque! He has nearly beaten me to death!” Friar Sand and Bajie asked, “Which macaque was it?” The elder said nothing and merely sighed. After asking for water and drinking a few mouthfuls, he finally said, “Disciples, just after you left, Wukong came back to pester me again. I steadfastly refused to take him back, so he struck me with his staff and stole both bundles wrapped in blue felt.” Hearing this, Bajie ground his teeth and felt rage blaze in his heart. “That damned, wretched monkey! How dare he behave so outrageously?” He said, “Friar Sand, attend to Master while I go to his home and demand the bundles back.” Friar Sand said, “Do not be angry yet. Let us first help Master to that household in the hollow, beg some hot tea or broth, warm up the rice we obtained earlier, and nurse Master back to strength. Then we can go look for him.”

p.src: Bajie did as he was told, helping the Master onto the horse; then, carrying the alms bowl with the cold rice bundled inside, he went straight to the door of the house. They saw that only an old woman was at home, and at the sudden sight of them she hurriedly shrank away. Shajing joined his palms and said, “Good mother, we have been sent from the Tang realm in the Eastern Land to journey to the Western Heaven. Our Master is somewhat unwell, so we have called at your honored house especially to beg a little hot tea or broth for him to take with his rice.” The old woman said, “A moment ago there was a gluttonous monk here who said he had been sent from the Eastern Land. He has already gone off after receiving alms. How can there be another party from the Eastern Land? There is no one else at home, so please try elsewhere.” When the elder heard this, he leaned on Bajie, dismounted, bowed, and said, “Good mother, I have three disciples who have been united in heart and purpose in protecting me on my way to the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the land of India, there to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. But my senior disciple, whose name is Sun Wukong, has been fierce and cruel all his life and refuses to follow the path of goodness, so I sent him back. I never expected him to come secretly after us, strike me across the back with his cudgel, and rob me of our luggage, robes, and alms bowl. Now I must send one of my disciples to find him and recover them; but as that open road is no place to sit and wait, I have come especially to your house to rest here for a while. As soon as the disciple returns with the luggage, we shall leave and certainly will not dare remain long.” The old woman said, “Just now a sallow, plump, gluttonous monk came to beg food. He too said he was traveling from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven. How can there be another group?” Bajie could not help laughing. “That was me. Because I was born with a long snout and great ears, I feared your household would be frightened and refuse me food, so I changed myself into that appearance. If you do not believe me, is that not the scorched rice from your own pot in my brother’s robe?”

p.src: The old woman recognized that it was indeed the rice she had given him, so she no longer turned them away and let them sit down. She then heated a pot of tea and handed it to Shajing to pour over the rice. Shajing promptly soaked the cold rice in it and handed it to the Master. After the Master had eaten a few mouthfuls and composed himself for some time, he asked, “Who will go and recover the luggage?” Bajie said, “The year before last, when Master sent him away, I went to look for him once, so I know his Water-Curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain. Let me go. Let me go.” The elder said, “You must not go. That macaque has never got along with you, and you speak coarsely besides. If one or two words should go amiss between you, he will strike you. Let Wujing go.” Shajing agreed, saying, “I will go. I will go.” The elder further instructed Shajing, “When you arrive, be sure to judge how matters stand. If he is willing to give you the bundle, offer him some courteous thanks and bring it back. If he refuses, on no account contend with him. Go directly to the Bodhisattva in the Southern Sea, tell her what has happened, and ask her to demand it from him.” Shajing obeyed every instruction. He said to Bajie, “I am going to find him now. Whatever you do, do not grumble or make trouble; take good care of the Master. Nor must you behave outrageously in this household, lest they refuse to provide you with food. I shall return as soon as I have gone.” Bajie nodded and said, “I understand. Go on, then. Whether you recover it or not, come back early. Do not end up like a pointed carrying pole that loses its load from both ends.” Shajing then formed the magic sign, mounted a radiant cloud, and headed straight for the Eastern Continent of Superior Body. Indeed:

p.src: Shajing traveled through the air for three days and nights before reaching the Eastern Ocean, where suddenly he heard the sound of the waves. Looking down, he saw in truth black mist swelling to the heavens as the gloomy vapors thickened, while the vast sea held the sun and chilled the light of dawn. He had no heart to admire the view, but headed toward the immortal mountain, crossed Yingzhou, and went due east until he reached the borders of Flower-Fruit Mountain. Riding the sea wind and treading the force of the waters, he traveled on for a long while until he saw lofty peaks arrayed like halberds and sheer cliffs hanging like screens. Reaching the peak, he brought down his cloud, found the path down the mountain, and searched for the Water-Curtain Cave. As he drew near, he heard countless monkey spirits clamoring noisily in the mountain. Shajing went closer and looked carefully. There was Pilgrim Sun seated high upon a stone platform, holding a sheet of paper in both hands and reading aloud in a ringing voice:

p.src: When Shajing heard that it was the travel warrant, he could restrain himself no longer. Stepping forward, he shouted sternly, “Elder Brother, why are you reading the Master’s travel warrant?” At these words Pilgrim quickly raised his head, pretended not to recognize Shajing, and cried, “Seize him! Seize him!” The monkeys surrounded Shajing all at once, tugged and dragged him forward, and demanded, “Who are you, to dare approach our immortal cave without leave?” Seeing that Pilgrim had changed his manner and refused to recognize him, Shajing had no choice but to salute him and say, “I beg leave to report to Elder Brother: what happened before was truly that the Master lost his temper and wrongly blamed you. He recited the spell against you several times and drove you home. For one thing, we younger disciples did not remonstrate and reconcile you; for another, we had gone to seek water and beg food because the Master was hungry and thirsty. We never expected you to return out of goodwill, only to resent the Master for rigidly refusing to keep you; and so you struck him down and left him unconscious on the ground. Then you carried off the luggage. Afterward we revived the Master, and I have come especially to pay my respects to you. If you bear the Master no hatred, then remember his former kindness in freeing you, and come with me and the luggage to see him. Let us journey together to the Western Heaven and attain the true fruit of our labors. But if your resentment runs too deep and you refuse to come, then by all means grant me the bundle. You may enjoy the peaceful evening of your life here in the deep mountains, and thus both sides will gain what they desire.”

p.src: When Pilgrim heard this, he gave a cold chuckle. “Worthy Brother, that argument does not please me at all. I struck the Tang Monk and seized the luggage neither because I have no wish to go west nor because I love living here. Now that I have thoroughly studied the travel document, I shall go west myself to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures, then deliver them to the Eastern Land. I alone shall achieve the merit, and the people of the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa will honor me as their patriarch, preserving my name for ten thousand generations.” Shajing laughed. “Elder Brother, what you say is not quite right. Since ancient times there has never been any tale of Sun Wukong fetching the scriptures. Our Buddha, the Tathagata, created the true scriptures of the Three Baskets and expressly sent the Bodhisattva Guanyin to the Eastern Land to find a scripture pilgrim. We were charged to endure the hardships of a thousand mountains, travel through many lands, and protect that pilgrim. The Bodhisattva once told us that the scripture pilgrim was a disciple of the Tathagata named Elder Golden Cicada. Because he failed to listen to the Buddha expound the scriptures, he was banished from Spirit Mountain and reborn in the Eastern Land, so that he might attain the true fruit in the West and cultivate the Great Way anew. The demonic trials he was destined to meet along the road brought about the release of the three of us, that we might serve as his guardians. If you go without the Tang Monk, what Buddha would be willing to transmit the scriptures to you? Would that not make all your scheming and effort entirely vain?” Pilgrim said, “Worthy Brother, you are truly muddleheaded: you know the one but not the other. You imagine that because you have a Tang Monk for you to protect, I have no Tang Monk of my own? I have chosen another true monk of great virtue who is here with me and will go to fetch the scriptures himself. What is wrong with old Sun supporting him single-handed? We have already chosen to set out early tomorrow morning. If you do not believe me, wait while I summon him for you to see.” He called, “Little ones, quickly invite the venerable Master out here.” Sure enough, they ran inside, led out a white horse, and ushered forth a Tang Sanzang. Behind him came a Bajie carrying the luggage. And there was a Shajing holding a monk’s staff.

p.src: When Sha Wujing saw this, he flew into a rage and cried, “I, Old Sha, never change my name whether walking or sitting. How can there be another Monk Sha here? Take that for your insolence!” The valiant Sha Wujing raised his Demon-Quelling Staff in both hands and struck the false Sha Wujing dead with a blow to the head. It proved to be a monkey spirit. The Pilgrim grew furious. Brandishing his gold-banded cudgel, he led the host of monkeys in surrounding Sha Wujing. Sha Wujing charged east and west until he broke through their lines, then mounted the clouds and mist to escape, saying, “That damned monkey is behaving outrageously. I shall report him to the Bodhisattva.” Seeing that Sha Wujing had killed one monkey spirit and that they had driven Monk Sha away, the Pilgrim made no attempt to pursue him. He returned to the cave and ordered his underlings to drag the dead fiend’s body aside, skin it, and fry its flesh. Then he and all the monkeys feasted on it with coconut wine and grape wine. He chose another demon monkey skilled in transformation, changed him into another Monk Sha, and began drilling them anew for the journey west. Of this we speak no further.

p.src: Sha Wujing rode a cloud away from the Eastern Ocean and, after traveling for a day and a night, reached the Southern Ocean. As he traveled on, he soon saw that Mount Luojia was not far away. He hastened forward, lowered his cloud and mist, and looked about. What a splendid place it was! Truly it was:

He hastened forward, lowered his cloud and mist, and looked about. What a splendid place it was!
Truly it was:

p.src: Sha Wujing walked slowly over Mount Luojia, admiring the immortal realm. He then saw the Pilgrim Moksha coming to meet him. “Sha Wujing,” Moksha said, “why have you come here instead of protecting the Tang Monk on his scripture pilgrimage?” After making his obeisance, Sha Wujing said, “I have come especially to see the Bodhisattva about a certain matter. Please be so kind as to announce me.” Moksha knew that he had come in search of the Pilgrim, but said nothing of it. He went in first and reported to the Bodhisattva, “The Tang Monk’s youngest disciple, Sha Wujing, is outside to pay his respects.” Sun the Pilgrim, hearing this from below the terrace, laughed and said, “The Tang Monk must be in trouble, and Sha Wujing has come to ask the Bodhisattva for help.” The Bodhisattva immediately ordered Moksha to summon him inside. Sha Wujing prostrated himself and bowed. When he raised his head and was about to recount what had happened, he suddenly saw Sun the Pilgrim standing nearby. Without waiting to speak, he whipped out his Demon-Quelling Staff and struck straight at the Pilgrim’s face. The Pilgrim did not strike back, but drew aside and dodged the blow. Sha Wujing cursed wildly, “You damned monkey, guilty of the ten abominations and of rebellion! Now you have come to deceive the Bodhisattva too!” The Bodhisattva shouted, “Wujing, do not fight. Tell me first what has happened.”

p.src: Sha Wujing put away his precious staff and bowed again below the terrace. Seething with anger, he said to the Bodhisattva, “That monkey has committed more acts of violence along the road than can be counted. The day before yesterday, at the foot of a mountain slope, he killed two highway robbers, and Master reproached him for it. Unexpectedly, that very night we lodged at the robbers’ leader’s house, where he beat the whole band of robbers to death without mercy. Then he brought back a blood-drenched human head to show Master. Master was so frightened that he fell from his horse. He cursed the monkey a few times and drove him away to return here. After they parted, Master became desperately hungry and thirsty, and sent Bajie to look for water. When Bajie did not return after a long wait, Master sent me to look for him too. Unexpectedly, Sun the Pilgrim saw that the two of us were away, returned, struck Master with his iron cudgel, and stole the two bundles wrapped in blue felt. When we returned, we revived Master, and I came especially to his Water Curtain Cave to find him and demand the bundles back. But to my surprise, he had turned hostile and refused to acknowledge me, while reading Master’s travel rescript over and over. I asked him why he was reading it, and he said that he would no longer protect the Tang Monk. He meant to go to the Western Heaven for the scriptures himself, deliver them to the land of the East, claim the merit as his own, be established as a patriarch, and have his name celebrated for all ages. Then I said, ‘Without the Tang Monk, who would be willing to hand the scriptures over to you?’ He replied that he had chosen a true monk possessed of the Way. When they were summoned, there indeed appeared a white horse and a Tang Monk, with Bajie and Sha Wujing following behind. I said, ‘I am Monk Sha. How can there be another Monk Sha here?’ I rushed forward and struck him with my precious staff, whereupon he proved to be a monkey spirit. He then led the whole mob to seize me, and so I have come especially to lodge my complaint and seek the Bodhisattva’s aid. I did not know that he could use the Somersault Cloud and arrive here before me. Nor do I know what artful lies and honeyed words he has used to deceive the Bodhisattva.” The Bodhisattva said, “Wujing, do not accuse others falsely. Wukong arrived here four days ago, and I have never once allowed him to go back. How could he have conceived the intention of choosing another Tang Monk and fetching the scriptures on his own?” Sha Wujing said, “At this very moment there is a Sun the Pilgrim in the Water Curtain Cave. How would I dare deceive you?” The Bodhisattva said, “If that is so, do not be impatient. I shall have Wukong accompany you to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit to investigate. If the other is genuine, he will be hard to destroy; if false, he will be easy to eliminate. Once you arrive, the truth will reveal itself.”

The Bodhisattva said, “Wujing, do not accuse others falsely.
Wukong arrived here four days ago, and I have never once allowed him to go back. How could he have conceived the intention of choosing another Tang Monk and fetching the scriptures on his own?”
Sha Wujing said, “At this very moment there is a Sun the Pilgrim in the Water Curtain Cave. How would I dare deceive you?”

The Bodhisattva said, “If that is so, do not be impatient. I shall have Wukong accompany you to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit to investigate. If the other is genuine, he will be hard to destroy; if false, he will be easy to eliminate. Once you arrive, the truth will reveal itself.”
